metadata.title: Product Streams
metadata.description: Outcome-based product streams for the Internal Developer Platform domain, centered on developer self-service, runtime foundations, secure delivery, and engineering insight.

definitions.productBrick: A reusable implementation-facing building block used to realize one or more product streams.
definitions.productStream: A high-level, outcome-based experience that delivers customer or business value.

metadata.flowModelNote: Each experience now carries only experience-specific flows. Each flow step lists the bricks and external systems used inside that experience.

rootGroups.name: Developer Journey
rootGroups.description: Streams that help engineers and engineering leads find the right platform path, start work quickly, and see where developer flow is improving or degrading.

streams.name: Find the Right Platform Path
streams.description: Help developers understand which services, standards, and ownership boundaries apply to their work.

flows.title: Find the Right Platform Path
flows.description: Help developers understand which services, standards, and ownership boundaries apply to their work.

steps.title: Open developer portal
keyFacts: The portal is the main entry point for platform discovery, ownership lookup, and self-service actions.
Engineers need current catalog metadata before they can choose a supported path confidently.
painPoints: Stale service ownership or scattered docs push teams back to chat-driven support.
If the portal hides support status or lifecycle state, teams cannot tell which path is safe to adopt.

dependencies.name: Developer Portal and Service Catalog
dependencies.description: The front door to the platform, combining service catalog metadata, documentation, ownership, templates, and self-service actions.
dependencies.how: Uses Developer Portal and Service Catalog for the front door to the platform, combining service catalog metadata, documentation, ownership, templates, and self-service actions in open developer portal.

steps.title: Find service template
keyFacts: Template choice shapes the service architecture, delivery defaults, and ongoing support model.
Developers need templates organized by workload type, maturity, and operational expectations.
painPoints: Noisy template lists create false starts and inconsistent service scaffolds.
Teams lose trust when template guidance does not explain limits, prerequisites, or ownership.

dependencies.name: Developer Portal and Service Catalog
dependencies.description: The front door to the platform, combining service catalog metadata, documentation, ownership, templates, and self-service actions.
dependencies.how: Uses Developer Portal and Service Catalog for the front door to the platform, combining service catalog metadata, documentation, ownership, templates, and self-service actions in find service template.

steps.title: Check ownership and standards
keyFacts: Ownership, lifecycle state, and required standards have to be visible before a team commits to a platform path.
Standards are easier to follow when they are expressed as concrete checks and examples.
painPoints: Hidden control requirements surface late as release blockers.
Unclear ownership forces teams to negotiate exceptions before they understand the default path.

dependencies.name: Developer Portal and Service Catalog

steps.title: Choose platform path
keyFacts: The final path choice should connect the service definition, template, runtime, and support model.
A good choice reduces future migration work and makes platform expectations explicit.
painPoints: Teams create bespoke setups when the recommended path does not fit visible constraints.
Weak decision guidance leads to avoidable rework in delivery, security, and operations.

streams.description: Help developers bootstrap services with the right templates, tooling, and repo setup.

flows.description: Help developers bootstrap services with the right templates, tooling, and repo setup.

steps.title: Generate service template
keyFacts: Template generation is where platform standards become concrete files, workflows, and ownership metadata.
The generated baseline should include enough defaults to run locally and enter CI without extra negotiation.
painPoints: Incomplete scaffolds send engineers into manual setup before they have confidence in the path.
Generated code loses credibility when it is not kept current with runtime and policy expectations.

steps.title: Set up local workspace
keyFacts: Local workspace setup determines how quickly an engineer reaches the first useful feedback loop.
Consistent IDE, container, and CLI defaults reduce support load across teams.
painPoints: Machine-specific setup steps create hidden variance that only appears later in CI or production.
Opaque failures make engineers bypass the supported tooling instead of improving it.

dependencies.name: IDE Workspace and Local Developer Tooling
dependencies.description: Provides the local engineering entry point through IDE setup, workspace bootstrapping, dev containers, local runtime helpers, and supported command-line workflows.

steps.title: Create repository baseline
keyFacts: Repository defaults establish ownership, review, branch, security, and automation expectations from day one.
A useful baseline connects source control with catalog metadata and delivery workflows.
painPoints: Missing repository policies become expensive to retrofit after the team starts shipping.
Unclear code ownership or review rules slow the first production change.

steps.title: Start development flow
keyFacts: The first development loop should prove that local tooling, source control, and CI are aligned.
Fast feedback matters more than feature breadth at this point in the journey.
painPoints: Engineers lose momentum when the first test, build, or pull request requires platform support.
Small inconsistencies between local and CI behavior create early distrust in the paved road.

streams.name: See and Improve Flow
streams.description: Help developers and platform teams identify friction in daily engineering workflows.

flows.title: See and Improve Flow
flows.description: Help developers and platform teams identify friction in daily engineering workflows.

steps.title: Review workflow telemetry
keyFacts: Workflow telemetry should show where teams wait, retry, or leave the supported path.
Managers and platform teams need trends they can connect to concrete platform changes.
painPoints: Raw activity data is hard to act on without segmentation by team, workflow, and platform stream.
Delayed or untrusted metrics push investment decisions back toward anecdotes.

steps.title: Identify bottleneck
keyFacts: A bottleneck is useful only when it can be tied to an owned workflow, service, or platform brick.
Assistant workflows can summarize recurring friction when they operate within approved data and action boundaries.
painPoints: Unexplained recommendations create more debate than action.
Telemetry that cannot distinguish platform friction from team practice leads to the wrong fix.

steps.title: Compare team flow
keyFacts: Team comparisons should normalize for workflow type and maturity so the signal is fair.
The goal is to find transferable practices and platform gaps, not rank teams out of context.
painPoints: Scoreboard-style reporting damages trust when it ignores service complexity or incident load.
Teams disengage when they cannot trace a metric back to a change they control.

dependencies.name: Agentic Engineering and Coding Assistants

dependencies.how: Uses Agentic Engineering and Coding Assistants for AI-assisted coding, code explanation, workflow automation, and agent-driven engineering actions inside approved platform boundaries in compare team flow.

steps.title: Adjust engineering practice
keyFacts: Telemetry becomes valuable when it changes templates, docs, defaults, or team practices.
Follow-up actions should be tracked until they reduce the measured friction.
painPoints: Insights decay when no team owns the resulting platform or practice change.
One-off coaching does not scale unless the learning is fed back into the paved road.

rootGroups.name: Delivery Journey
rootGroups.description: Streams that move code, artifacts, environments, and releases through trusted platform paths with less handoff and less local reinvention.

streams.name: Build and Store Artifacts Safely
streams.description: Help engineers produce trusted build outputs and make them available across environments.

flows.title: Build and Store Artifacts Safely
flows.description: Help engineers produce trusted build outputs and make them available across environments.

steps.title: Build artifact
keyFacts: Build outputs need provenance, repeatability, and compatible base images before they can be trusted downstream.
Artifact metadata should travel with the build into scan, promotion, and deployment workflows.
painPoints: Unreproducible builds make incident response and rollback slower.
Missing provenance forces manual review before artifacts can move to protected environments.

steps.title: Scan artifact
keyFacts: Security, license, and quality scans should run early enough to fix issues before release pressure rises.
Findings need clear severity, ownership, and exception paths.
painPoints: Late or noisy findings teach teams to ignore the scanner.
Unclear remediation guidance shifts work from automation back to security support queues.

dependencies.name: Artifact Supply Chain and Base Images

Consumers need confidence that registry state matches the release record.
painPoints: Ambiguous tags and inconsistent retention make rollback risky.
Weak registry permissions let unsupported artifacts enter the delivery path.

streams.name: Release with Confidence
streams.description: Help engineering teams move changes through pipelines and promotion steps with less manual risk.

flows.title: Release with Confidence
flows.description: Help engineering teams move changes through pipelines and promotion steps with less manual risk.

steps.title: Run delivery pipeline
keyFacts: The standard pipeline should make build, test, scan, and deploy status understandable in one flow.
Reusable pipeline actions reduce local maintenance while keeping audit evidence consistent.
painPoints: Pipeline failures become support tickets when logs and next actions are hard to interpret.
Teams maintain bespoke pipelines when the shared library cannot express common release needs.

dependencies.name: Delivery Pipelines and Release Automation
dependencies.description: Reusable build, test, deploy, promote, and rollback workflows that encode the expected delivery path.
dependencies.how: Uses Delivery Pipelines and Release Automation for reusable build, test, deploy, promote, and rollback workflows that encode the expected delivery path in run delivery pipeline.

steps.title: Promote release
keyFacts: Promotion should depend on explicit evidence, policy state, and environment readiness.
The release path needs clear approvals, automated gates, and auditable state transitions.
painPoints: Manual promotion steps create drift between environments.
Ambiguous gate failures cause release managers to bypass or duplicate checks.

dependencies.name: Delivery Pipelines and Release Automation
dependencies.description: Reusable build, test, deploy, promote, and rollback workflows that encode the expected delivery path.
dependencies.how: Uses Delivery Pipelines and Release Automation for reusable build, test, deploy, promote, and rollback workflows that encode the expected delivery path in promote release.

steps.title: Review deployment result
keyFacts: Deployment review should connect rollout state, health signals, release evidence, and ownership in one decision point.
Teams need a clear view of whether to continue, pause, roll back, or escalate.
painPoints: A green deployment step can still hide service health or dependency regressions.
Disconnected rollout and telemetry views slow down release decisions.

dependencies.name: Continuous Delivery and Deployment Promotion

dependencies.how: Uses Continuous Delivery and Deployment Promotion for deployment promotion, progressive delivery, environment synchronization, and release-state control after CI has produced approved artifacts in review deployment result.

steps.title: Rollback or continue
keyFacts: Rollback and continue decisions should preserve the evidence behind the choice.
A reliable rollback path is part of release design, not an exceptional manual procedure.
painPoints: Teams hesitate when rollback effects on data, dependencies, or downstream services are unclear.
Missing release history turns recovery into incident improvisation.

painPoints: Free-form requests become ticket queues in another interface.
Teams overprovision when environment options and costs are not visible.

painPoints: Partial provisioning leaves teams with environments they cannot safely use or tear down.
Hidden dependencies make environment creation unpredictable under load.

Manual preview cleanup creates cloud waste and stale test surfaces.

Teams avoid ephemeral environments when cleanup is manual or risky.

rootGroups.name: Secure Delivery Journey
rootGroups.description: Streams that embed quality, identity, policy, and runtime protection into delivery workflows so control improves without blocking normal work.

streams.name: Ship with Safe Defaults
streams.description: Help developers catch quality and access issues before they become delivery problems.

flows.title: Ship with Safe Defaults
flows.description: Help developers catch quality and access issues before they become delivery problems.

steps.title: Run code checks
keyFacts: Code checks should run close to the pull request and explain what must change before merge.
Findings need to distinguish advisory guidance from blocking policy.
painPoints: Noisy checks slow teams down and reduce respect for important controls.
Rules that differ between local and CI workflows create avoidable rework.

dependencies.name: Code Quality and Static Analysis
dependencies.description: Runs static analysis, code-quality checks, dependency review, and source-level engineering standards before code reaches the wider delivery path.
dependencies.how: Uses Code Quality and Static Analysis for runs static analysis, code-quality checks, dependency review, and source-level engineering standards before code reaches the wider delivery path in run code checks.

steps.title: Resolve access issue
keyFacts: Access issues should be resolved through least-privilege workflows with clear ownership and audit evidence.
The fastest path should still preserve identity and secret-management standards.
painPoints: Manual access fixes become long-lived permissions when expiry is not enforced.
Unclear access ownership pushes engineers into broad exception requests.

steps.title: Handle secret usage safely
keyFacts: Secret usage should follow approved delivery and runtime patterns without copying sensitive values into local workflows.
Developers need safe examples for common service and integration cases.
painPoints: Secret handling becomes risky when documentation is generic or split across tools.
Local workarounds can leak into production configuration.

dependencies.name: Identity, Secrets and Access Guardrails
dependencies.description: Provides workload identity, secret delivery, least-privilege defaults, and access-control patterns used across the platform.
dependencies.how: Uses Identity, Secrets and Access Guardrails for workload identity, secret delivery, least-privilege defaults, and access-control patterns used across the platform in handle secret usage safely.

steps.title: Merge with policy guardrails
keyFacts: Merge should show policy state, required evidence, and exception options before the final decision.
Guardrails work best when they are predictable and explainable in the review flow.
painPoints: Surprise merge blockers create pressure to bypass controls.
Policy exceptions become unmanageable when they are not linked to code, owner, and expiry.

flows.description: Help platform and security teams apply policy and runtime protections with enough developer empathy to stay usable.

steps.title: Publish policy
keyFacts: Policies need owners, rationale, severity, rollout mode, and tested examples before broad enforcement.
Publishing should separate warn, block, and exception states.
painPoints: Controls that appear without context create avoidable resistance from product teams.
Untested policies can block safe releases or miss risky ones.

steps.title: Review policy violation
keyFacts: Violation review should show affected services, owners, evidence, and recommended remediation.
Reviewers need enough context to distinguish urgent risk from acceptable temporary variance.
painPoints: Sparse findings force security teams into manual investigation.
Overloaded violation queues delay real risk reduction.

dependencies.name: Security Posture and Runtime Protection

dependencies.how: Uses Security Posture and Runtime Protection for workload posture assessment, runtime protection signals, and cross-platform security visibility beyond source-level or policy-only checks in review policy violation.

steps.title: Grant exception if needed
keyFacts: Exceptions should be explicit, time-bound, owner-approved, and visible to the teams that carry the risk.
A good exception path keeps delivery moving while preserving accountability.
painPoints: Permanent exceptions turn governance into documentation theater.
Slow exception reviews make teams work around the platform instead of using it.

dependencies.name: Policy as Code and Compliance Controls

dependencies.how: Uses Policy as Code and Compliance Controls for encodes engineering, security, and compliance requirements into reusable checks, evidence, and exception workflows in grant exception if needed.

steps.title: Track runtime posture
keyFacts: Runtime posture should connect deployed workload state with policy expectations and recent change history.
Security and reliability teams need trends, not just point-in-time findings.
painPoints: Disconnected runtime findings are difficult to prioritize or assign.
Posture data loses credibility when it lags behind actual deployments.

flows.title: Understand Service Health

steps.title: Open observability view
keyFacts: The first observability view should show service health, ownership, dependencies, and recent changes together.
Engineers need a consistent starting point before switching into specialist tools.
painPoints: Scattered dashboards delay triage and create conflicting interpretations.
Missing ownership or dependency context slows the first response.

Useful alerts lead directly to logs, traces, runbooks, and recent deployment context.
painPoints: Noisy alerts train teams to delay response.
Alerts without service context force responders to reconstruct the situation manually.

dependencies.description: Shared logging, metrics, tracing, alerting, and dashboarding foundation used across services and platform workflows.
dependencies.how: Uses Observability and Telemetry Foundation for shared logging, metrics, tracing, alerting, and dashboarding foundation used across services and platform workflows in investigate alert.

steps.title: Trace failing request
keyFacts: Tracing should reveal the failing path across service, dependency, and platform boundaries.
A good trace helps teams decide whether the issue is application, platform, or external dependency behavior.
painPoints: Sampling gaps and inconsistent instrumentation hide the actual failure path.
Engineers lose time when trace, log, and metric dimensions do not line up.

keyFacts: Incident coordination needs ownership, severity, communications, rollback options, and follow-up actions in one workflow.
Automation should reduce coordination overhead without hiding judgment calls.
painPoints: Incident state fragments across chat, tickets, dashboards, and release tools.
Post-incident fixes are missed when follow-up work is not tied back to platform bricks and templates.

streams.name: See Cost and Capacity Tradeoffs
streams.description: Help engineering leads understand cost and capacity implications of the systems they run.

flows.title: See Cost and Capacity Tradeoffs
flows.description: Help engineering leads understand cost and capacity implications of the systems they run.

steps.title: Review cost trend
keyFacts: Cost trends need attribution to services, teams, environments, and platform streams.
Leads need enough history to separate growth, waste, and planned investment.
painPoints: Unattributed spend turns cost review into argument instead of action.
Monthly-only reporting is too slow for rapidly growing runtime usage.

dependencies.name: Cost, Capacity and Usage Insights
dependencies.description: Provides cost, capacity, adoption, and value signals that help teams understand the economic effect of platform usage and runtime decisions.
dependencies.how: Uses Cost, Capacity and Usage Insights for cost, capacity, adoption, and value signals that help teams understand the economic effect of platform usage and runtime decisions in review cost trend.

steps.title: Compare service usage
keyFacts: Usage comparison should normalize for traffic, service criticality, and environment lifecycle.
Good comparisons reveal reusable optimization patterns without shaming teams.
painPoints: Raw spend comparisons punish high-value services and miss waste in low-traffic ones.
Teams cannot act when the report does not show the architecture or platform decision behind the cost.

steps.title: Spot capacity pressure
keyFacts: Capacity pressure should combine utilization, performance, reliability, and planned demand signals.
Teams need early warning before scaling limits become incidents or expensive emergency work.
painPoints: Capacity signals buried in infrastructure dashboards do not reach product decision makers.
Late pressure detection forces rushed scaling choices and avoidable cost.

steps.title: Decide optimization action
keyFacts: Optimization decisions should balance cost, reliability, delivery risk, and developer effort.
Actions need owners, expected savings, guardrails, and a way to verify the result.
painPoints: Cost-cutting without reliability context creates hidden operational risk.
Optimization ideas stall when savings and engineering effort are not visible together.
